This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel econometric framework designed for modeling and forecasting count time series. We demonstrate that the score-driven approach is ideal for tracking the evolution of time-varying parameters, offering the necessary flexibility to handle count data with complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. Under mild conditions, we establish the asymptotic properties of the TV-PARX model, proving that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) produces parameter estimates that are both strongly consistent and asymptotically normal. Monte Carlo simulations are used to assess finite-sample performance and forecasting precision. Furthermore, the practical value of the TV-PARX model's time-varying specification is illustrated through an analysis of daily new COVID-19 infections in Italy and corporate defaults in the United States. To facilitate research in this area, we have made the R package implementing the TV-PARX model accessible via CRAN at the following URL: https://github.com/giacomob/TVPARX.
Although the concept of employing stellar photometry to monitor the atmosphere for high-energy astrophysics optical experiments appears simple, achieving the high precision required to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) to within 0.01 has been challenging. Wide-field photometry spanning various altitudes enables a rapid, calibration-independent VAOD calculation, while simultaneously serving as a valuable calibration by-product. By leveraging multi-year datasets from the FRAM (F/(Ph)otometric Robotic Atmospheric Monitor) telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina and approximately one year of data from a comparable instrument at the future Cherenkov Telescope Array site in Chile, we have refined measurement techniques to enhance precision, potentially surpassing the 0.01 threshold. Crucially, this analysis relied on detailed laboratory assessments of the system's response to light spectrum and intensity, as the standard assumption of CCD detector linearity no longer holds under these specific observational conditions. Utilizing a calibrated approach that integrates simultaneous two-wavelength photometry to isolate atmospheric extinction, we employed a stepwise regression method to identify and account for additional non-linear effects influencing the residual calibration. These findings offer significant guidance for deploying single-channel photometric systems at high altitudes to estimate VAOD as a screening tool for the optical sensitivity of distant large-telescope facilities. Furthermore, this work establishes a framework applicable to other high-precision calibration challenges involving CCD detectors in atmospheric conditions that introduce non-linear variations.

This study evaluates and compares numerous numerical techniques for addressing stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics, which rely on combinations of deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. Leveraging recent work by the authors, the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion is employed to analyze sampling accuracy and quantify stepsize-dependent biases in configurational averaging. For harmonic oscillators, specific schemes yield exact configurational averaging, potentially enhancing the modeling of biomolecules where bond stretching is critical. In general systems, an optimal method is identified that exhibits significantly lower bias than alternatives. Simulations of the alanine dipeptide (both solvated and unsolvated) demonstrate that this approach achieves higher accuracy without sacrificing computational efficiency, supports larger timesteps, and maintains the conformational exploration rate. The proposed scheme represents a uniformly superior algorithm for molecular sampling, offering practical timestep increases of over 25% in vacuum and reducing errors in configurational averages by more than a factor of ten in solvated simulations at large timesteps. As an improved standard, it enables more accurate free energy calculations and other processes where systematic errors previously accumulated. The proposed scheme represents a significant advancement in molecular sampling, practically increasing timesteps by over 25% in vacuum simulations and reducing errors in configurational means by more than ten times in solvated simulations at large timesteps. As an enhanced benchmark, this approach facilitates more precise free energy computations and other tasks previously hindered by systematic errors. In practical applications, this represents a substantial leap forward for molecular simulations. Utilizing the Euler-, Midpoint-, or Heun-method together with the Brownian Brownian-term (BB-term) constitutes another viable configuration worth considering.

Therefore, it is essential to estimate these errors and assess whether the timesteps and model approximations employed remain within acceptable limits. Current automatic image description models are typically trained and assessed using crowdsourced human-generated captions, with system performance measured by similarity metrics such as BLEU, Meteor, and CIDER. Consequently, the reliability of both the systems and their evaluation hinges on the quality of these reference descriptions. As demonstrated in Section 2, existing image description datasets lack sufficient quality. I contend that more detailed guidelines are necessary, ones that balance the specific requirements of visually impaired users with the practical feasibility of generating appropriate descriptions. While high-quality data would allow for reference-based evaluation, we should also explore alternative assessment methods. These could involve comparing systems on their ability to prioritize information in answers to implicit questions posed by users or by human reviewers rating the utility of generated descriptions for specific tasks. Ultimately, the ultimate goal of a systems' utility should serve as the primary evaluation criterion. Fortunately, recent deep learning advancements could make it feasible to create larger, higher-quality data sets, potentially rendering reference-based evaluation feasible again.
Quantifying complexity within quantum field theory remains a formidable challenge, primarily due to the difficulty of moving past free models and their associated Gaussian states and operations. Our approach addresses this by examining conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, offering a comprehensive analysis of complexity for both states and operators within the universal sector of their energy-momentum tensor. Central to our framework are the Euler-Arnold equations and their integro-differential extensions, which ensure the optimization problem between arbitrary states or transformations is well-defined. This work expands upon the findings detailed in arXiv:2005.02415, elaborating on the derivation techniques employed. Key areas of focus include the application of differential regularization, solving the integro-differential equation governing Fubini-Study state complexity, and investigating the underlying geometric structure. Furthermore, we define a variational current related to the growth of state complexity and establish upper bounds based on forces analogous to those in the Born-Infeld model of holographic complexity. In the final sections, we integrate concepts from complexification into the operator framework, derive an area law for early-time growth, and outline potential directions for future research.
This section examines predictions from the bilepton model, an extension of the standard model where the gauge group shifts from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3) \times U(1)$ and fermion families are arranged non-sequentially, with the third family differing from the first two. To satisfy the requirements for triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom, the model necessitates exactly three families. The anticipated new physics comprises bileptons and three heavy quarks, ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. While QCD will bind these heavy quarks with light quarks and among themselves to create baryons and mesons, these composite particles will remain undetectable at the LHC but could be observed at a hypothetical 100 TeV proton-proton collider, unlike the bileptons. Distinguishing the underlying physics between baryons and mesons containing two heavy quarks at this 100 TeV collider will be challenging; thus, we focus primarily on the spectrum of baryons. We estimate production cross sections, decay modes, and decay chains for the first few baryons and mesons containing one, two, or three heavy quarks at both the 100 TeV collider and the LHC. It is important to note that while we provide estimates for production cross sections, decay modes, and final states for the lightest baryons and mesons with one, two, or three heavy quarks at a 100 TeV collider, determining the properties of the numerous higher-mass baryons and mesons that will also be produced at this collider represents a significant challenge. Conversely, all heavy quarks and the spectrum of baryons and mesons will generate signatures in proton-proton collisions at the LHC, primarily through the formation of top quark bound states (toponcs), which will be decays of the heavy bilepton. We conclude by discussing the implications for direct detection of topquark bound states at hadron colliders and topconcs at a future electron-positron collider.
This paper introduces IDET systems grounded in SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM, serving as the counterparts to our optimal wideband waveforming approach detailed in [1]. We formulate optimization problems aimed at maximizing both fair-throughput and sum-throughput. Leveraging a fixed-point based alternating algorithm, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput solutions for both SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM configurations. Subsequently, we demonstrate that the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput solutions utilize a time-multiplexed blend of ULink activation, data transmission, and training intervals. Finally, we establish the connectivity benefits of SFU-based wideband waveforming approaches across SISO, MISO, and SU MU-MISO frameworks. These findings validate the benefits of SFU-based wideband waveforming for multiuser systems and provide insights for future standard-setting initiatives regarding SFU benefits in multiuser environments. By contrast, the current IEEE 802.11ac standard operates as a SU MISO system that does not exploit SFU benefits for training or data transmission during uplink multiuser access. Furthermore, 5G New Air backhauls are expected to function on narrowband channels, likely utilizing SISO or MISO technologies.
Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) demands a unified framework that integrates extensive datasets from both theoretical predictions and experimental data. While data integration primarily involves standardizing formats, incorporating theoretical predictions is more complex due to the involvement of multiple components. Various independent groups develop distinct providers for different processes, utilizing diverse input parameters (runcards) and output structures (interpolation grids). Furthermore, because processes are measured across different scales, the PDF candidate requires DGLAP evolution, either calculated dynamically or precomputed into grids. Our goal is to automate all these steps within a single framework, making it a valuable resource for any PDF fitting group and potentially for broader phenomenological investigations. To achieve this, we employ a modular design with independent modules for reading runcards, managing PDF candidates (via dynamic DGLAP evolution and/or precomputed grids), calculating processes, and locating data points. This modularity allows groups to introduce new processes or data points without altering the core framework. We have implemented this approach in the open-source tool LovePDF (https://github.com/LovePDF/fittypdf), which has already been successfully applied to fit a wide range of datasets using CT18, MMT17, and ST14 starting points. In this presentation, we will outline the strategies used to handle runcards, evolution, process implementations, and data points, and we will demonstrate the framework's utility by comparing a minimal NNLO fit of a single dataset against a global analysis. Our conclusion will address potential future extensions. The implementation of typefinding for data points represents a significant challenge that has historically been managed through simple approximations; we will showcase how cvxpy enables an exact solution. Additionally, we will highlight the benefit of utilizing a public infrastructure like the HEPI grid for global fits, which can significantly reduce required computing resources.
This research conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent methane-air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An a priori analysis identified the linearized RANS-Eddy Break Up (EBU) model as the most appropriate choice for the specific setup, demonstrating high accuracy in reproducing LES-derived reaction rate fluctuations. Subsequently, the linearized governing equations, including the linearized EBU model for reaction rates, were solved for incoming acoustic perturbations. The resulting response modes indicate that reaction rate oscillations stem from Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings disturbing the jet flame. These findings align well with LES simulations regarding the mode shapes of both velocity and reaction rate fluctuations. Ultimately, a near-real-time control strategy based on the RANS-linearized EBU model offers a viable option for reacting flow control, potentially applicable for mitigating large-scale thermoacoustic instancies in power plant boilers.
Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, the constitutive relation incorporates two additional unknown functions: a nonlocal kernel and a mode of modification. These are constrained by empirical evidence; specifically, weak field observations support the causal kernel, while empirical support for the modified nature of NLG is drawn from binary pulsar data.
This presentation reports on selected recent LHC findings from the ALICE, ATLAS, and CMS experiments concerning small systems. Given that the study of high-multiplicity QCD in small systems has become a rapidly expanding area of significant interest to both the heavy-ion and broader high-energy physics communities, it is not feasible to cover all related topics in this paper. Instead, the discussion will focus on measurements addressing collective phenomena in small systems and recent results on strangeness enhancement in proton-proton collisions. Readers should be aware that many other intriguing results were excluded from this discussion due to space constraints. As the field of small system studies continues to develop, future publications will explore the topics omitted here. No conclusions regarding questions beyond the scope of this analysis are drawn in the following text.
The detection of certain variable X-ray sources in the Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date. Finally, we argue that the apparent lack of neutron star transients in the Galactic Centre is most plausibly explained by a genuine scarcity of such systems in that region, rather than by an extended transient recurrence time.
Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two separate sets of entities. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Furthermore, assuming the vertex size is bounded, we provide an algorithm that is fixed parameter tractable relative to both the number of edges and the number of vertices in the larger set. Finally, we propose an approximation algorithm capable of producing a planar drawing by splitting $O(\log e)$ edges, where $e$ represents the total count of edges. In addition, we detail an exact algorithm that maximizes the number of edges remaining undrawn in a planar visualization, and we develop a heuristic method for constructing near-optimal solutions. To facilitate the study of these issues, we have developed an open-source software library, which we applied to a dataset of relationships between software constructs and programming language constructs, resulting in multiple previously unknown planar drawings for construct pairs. This resource is accessible at https://github.com/Daveach/bipplan.
Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial complement to side-channel attacks. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel method that integrates prior strategies with simultaneous multithreading (SMT) architectures. Beyond this new technique, we identify a previously unrecognized source of slowdown by analyzing cache eviction as a root cause. The resulting performance degradation is substantially greater than previous methods, thereby enhancing the time granularity available for Flush+Reload attacks. We evaluated HyperDegrade across various Intel microarchitectures, achieving significant slowdowns that, in specific microbenchmark scenarios, represent a three-order-of-magnitude improvement over state-of-the-art solutions. To assess the effectiveness of performance degradation in amplifying side channels, we introduced and validated specific leakage metrics. Our findings indicate that HyperDegrade improves time granularity without compromising trace quality. Furthermore, we conducted a fair comparison of three performance degradation strategies when paired with Flush+Reload from an attacker's viewpoint. We also devised an attack targeting an underutilized vulnerability in OpenSSL, where HyperDegrade demonstrated superior performance by reducing the number of required Flush+Reload traces needed for success by a factor of three. In terms of cryptographic contributions, we revisited the recently proposed Raccoon attack on TLS-DH key exchanges, extending its application to other protocols. Leveraging HyperDegrade, we constructed an end-to-end attack proving that Raccoon-like exploits can succeed with real data, addressing a gap left by earlier research. As a final validation of our approach's practicality, we constructed a real-world attack utilizing HyperDegrade to almost fully factorize a three-order-of-magnitude strong private key through a remote side channel. Our findings suggest that existing mitigation strategies, such as performance noise, may be insufficient, and that system architects must consider more robust solutions. Furthermore, protocol designers need to reevaluate protocols like TLS-DH, potentially exploring alternative key exchange mechanisms. Regarding microarchitecture research, our study offers comprehensive insights into the microarchitectural foundations of HyperDegrade and its associated slowdowns. We characterized these foundations using microbenchmarks, employed assembly-level code analysis to understand their origins, and employed machine learning to predict them, all while considering different microarchitectural configurations. Finally, we concluded that HyperDegrade's effectiveness is most pronounced on Intel Skylake and older microarchitectures, as newer designs have mitigated many of the microarchitectural phenomena HyperDegrade exploits.
An unknotting operation represents a local modification applied to knot diagrams. It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. Finally, we calculate the diagonal distance for specific examples, illustrating the method's utility. The concepts and results presented here extend to wider categories of knot theories, including welded, regular, and shadow theories. Our approach offers an alternative to traditional unknotting operation studies, focusing on distinct local moves that transform any knot type into the unknot, rather than reducing complexity through successive unknotting operations on diagrams. These findings may prove valuable for future research in this area. Additionally, the study of diagonal distance in welded knots is directly relevant to the problem of determining the decidability of relations on regular languages associated with these distances; see [31, 32]. Our findings confirm the decidability for the diagonal distance, and we outline the strategy for adapting this result to other unknotting distances in regular, shadow, and other related theories. Coordination serves as a vital capability in multi-agent systems, enabling the completion of objectives that single agents cannot achieve alone. This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. We demonstrate that when prior distributions regarding task difficulty are diffuse, a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, intuitive linear structure emerges. Conversely, we find that if the prior distribution is not diffuse, an agent's best response to an affine strategy profile may become nonlinear. Furthermore, we present an algorithm capable of efficiently calculating a data-driven Nash equilibrium restricted to the class of affine policies. Through numerical experiments, we compare various equilibrium policies to highlight the approach's significance and practical value. These insights are applicable to scenarios involving a team of autonomous drones tasked with locating and rescuing missing individuals over a broad geographical area. The significance of multi-agent systems (MAS) lies in their ability to tackle complex challenges more effectively, efficiently, and reliably than isolated agents, while also offering robustness and continuity of service should individual agents fail [1], [2]. MAS find extensive applications across domains such as transportation [3], manufacturing [4], telecommunications [5], and autonomous teams [6]. Coordination constitutes a key function in MAS, particularly when teams face multiple tasks characterized by uncertain environments or competing goals [7]–[9]. Recent research has predominantly assumed that tasks follow specific probability distributions [10]–[13] or uniform distributions [14], [15], often relying on centralized controllers to determine actions based on system states or their distributions. However, in many real-world scenarios, task distributions remain unknown, and communication constraints limit access to a centralized controller. Consequently, there is growing interest in decentralized MAS operating under these conditions. For instance, consider a group of autonomous drones tasked with searching a large region for missing persons; the search density and duration for each location depend stochastically on how many drones are allocated there, yet this relationship remains unknown until sufficient search data is collected. Similarly, in smart manufacturing, the capacity of machines to process items might be uncertain, and no central entity has prior knowledge of these distributions. This paper demonstrates the embedding of regularly acting groups and diagonal groups into wreath products under their product action by utilizing Cartesian Decomposition. Additionally, the study derives the explicit form of Cartesian Decomposition for the wreath product acting in product action. Furthermore, the authors determine the centralizer of a specific element within the wreath product under product action, and this approach is applied to derive the explicit equations for Cartesian Decomposition for certain explicitly defined groups. Ultimately, these equations serve to identify the rank for the product action of the specified wreath product. These findings extend previous research concerning the explicit formulation of Cartesian Decomposition under product action. Additional outcomes and discussions related to product action, embedding, and Cartesian Decomposition are incorporated throughout the work. The investigations presented here align with and can be accessed at http://www.mathscinet.net/ar/abstract/26564.
The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise and ultimately by optical losses within the signal-recycling cavity. This limitation represents a primary barrier to detecting gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers in both current and future detectors, as it remains independent of arm length and the level of injected squeezing. In this study, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, derived from a Michelson interferometer by optically linking the end mirrors to form an additional cavity. This configuration creates a triply-coupled cavity system capable of surpassing the loss-induced high-frequency limit inherent to signal-recycled Michelson interferometers. Using parameters comparable to advanced LIGO+, a sloshing-Sagnac design could achieve sevenfold improved sensitivity at 2.5 kHz, or a fourfold increase in signal-to-noise ratio for typical post-merger binary neutron star waveforms. As an evolution of the Michelson architecture, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer offers a viable topology for upgrading current detectors and for future-generation observatories.

Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for delivering ultra-high data rates in environments with high user density. Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationarities and distinct visibility regions (VRs). These factors, combined with high UE density and limited pilot resources, make the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling algorithms particularly difficult. This paper introduces a joint RA and scheduling approach called the non-overlapping VR XL-MIMO (NOVR-XL) protocol. This method leverages the unique VRs of individual UEs to enhance RA performance and prioritizes scheduling UEs with non-overlapping VRs within the same payload data pilot resource. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed scheme yields substantial improvements in sum rate compared to conventional RA methods, while also lowering access latency and overall connectivity performance. These benefits are especially pronounced in environments characterized by very large XL-MIMO deployments and dense UE distributions.
Although neural language models have largely replaced traditional $N$-gram models due to superior performance, our findings suggest that $N$-grams still yield satisfactory results in many scenarios, effectively capturing significant linguistic knowledge at a low computational cost. Leveraging this insight, we propose training a neural model to predict the residuals between an $N$-gram model and the actual data distribution. This hybrid approach enables the neural component to concentrate on deeper linguistic understanding while offering a flexible framework for customization; one can switch the underlying $N$-gram model without retraining the neural component. Experiments across three standard tasks—language modeling, machine translation, and summarization—consistently show that our method outperforms existing standalone neural models. Furthermore, the approach facilitates effective domain adaptation by simply swapping in a domain-specific $N$-gram model, requiring no additional training. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.
This study investigates the performance of Informed OCR (iOCR), a system developed to correct errors in conventional OCR for vote tabulation using a spell correction algorithm. The findings indicate that iOCR outperforms traditional OCR methods. Notably, the mean error rate for image-based inputs decreased by 50%, while the rate of errors corrected by the system dropped an additional 25%. These results demonstrate that the algorithm effectively reduces both the volume and diversity of errors encountered when converting text into digital format. Leveraging these conclusions, we propose strategies to further enhance system performance. Additionally, we acknowledge limitations in the available data and suggest areas for future research. The source code and datasets for this study are accessible at https://github.com/ranjanp9999/iOCR.
This study investigates potential global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere using a simplified General Circulation Model (GCM) derived from the University of Hamburg's Portable University Model for the Atmosphere. The model incorporates simplified linear boundary layer friction, Newtonian cooling, and dry convective adjustment. Through a series of controlled experiments, researchers varied the planetary rotation rate and the imposed equator-to-pole temperature gradient. These variables were converted into dimensionless parameters to define a parameter space where distinct circulation regimes are identified and categorized. Significant trends emerge when altering the planetary rotation rate alongside frictional and thermal relaxation timescales. The progression of circulation regimes with respect to planetary rotation closely mirrors findings from laboratory studies on rotating, stratified fluids, particularly when topographic $\beta$-effects are included to simulate planetary vorticity gradients caused by spherical curvature. Additionally, a regular baroclinic wave regime appears at intermediate thermal Rossby numbers, with its characteristics and dominant zonal wavenumber heavily influenced by radiative and frictional damping strengths. These regular waves display notable similarities to baroclinic storms observed on Mars under specific conditions. At the highest rotation rates, multiple jets develop when the Rossby deformation radius and other eddy-related scales are significantly smaller than the planetary radius; these resemble the multiple zonal jets found on gas giant planets. These jets form on scales comparable to the most energetic eddies, poleward of the supercritical latitude, near the Rhines scale. Finally, the balance of heat transport between eddies and zonally symmetric flows varies significantly with rotation rate ($\Omega$), weakening as rotation accelerates. At lower rotation rates, eddies contribute more to heat transport, whereas zonally symmetric flows dominate at higher rotation rates. This shift occurs because eddy viscosity increases with rotation, dampening eddies, while zonally symmetric instabilities remain largely unaffected by eddy viscosity. These variations in heat transport imply different effective infrared emissivities required to keep the polar regions stable at high rotation rates, a factor that could have been crucial for enabling liquid water and life on super-Earths in the past. The characteristics of these circulation regimes depend on five dimensionless parameters: the topographic $\beta$-effect ($\beta L/U$), planetary vorticity gradient (Rossby $\beta$-parameter), rotation rate (Coriolis parameter), thermal Rossby number, and Rayleigh number. Understanding these characteristics and their formation mechanisms provides essential boundary conditions for GCMs used to explore Exoplanets and Mars
This study presents a real integral formulation for the reciprocal $\Gamma$ function using a regularized hypersingular integral. It confirms the equivalence between this new form and the standard complex representation, subsequently deriving a regularized complex expression that follows the conventional Hankel contour. The work further establishes identities connecting this regularized complex form to other known representations. Finally, the authors derive a series expansion on the positive real axis for the product of the new regularized hypersingular form and a power of a regularized finite-part integral; the convergence of this expansion is verified through a Hankel contour identity, ultimately yielding a series representation for the reciprocal $\Gamma$ function.
Hydrodynamic theories provide effective strategies for simulating the complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems that are otherwise computationally challenging. In this study, we develop a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method within the positive-P phase-space framework specifically for interacting Bose gases. This approach surpasses current hydrodynamic models, including superfluid and generalized hydrodynamics, by enabling the simulation of complete quantum dynamics; it can calculate non-equilibrium quantum correlations, even at short wavelengths. Based on this framework, we formulate a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme that extends the simulation duration for non-equilibrium scenarios beyond the limits of the full positive-P method, though this involves approximating quantum fluctuations. We demonstrate that this linearized scheme aligns directly with established Bogoliubov methods. Additionally, we validate the utility and benefits of this formalism by investigating correlations in a quantum shock wave scenario and contrasting its predictions with other standard quantum many-body approaches. To support future use, we release the implementation of this method open-source under the name StochHydro for the Julia programming language at https://github.com/danm15/StochHydro.
While Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at addressing large-scale problems across numerous domains, their deployment in real-time systems is often hindered by the sheer volume of parameters involved. To overcome this challenge, Teacher-Student architectures were initially introduced in the context of knowledge distillation, enabling lightweight student networks to match the performance of complex teacher models. Recently, these architectures have been widely adopted for diverse knowledge learning tasks, including knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Leveraging such frameworks, recent research has successfully achieved multiple learning objectives through efficient and compact student networks. Unlike previous surveys focused solely on knowledge distillation, this review comprehensively examines Teacher-Student architectures across a spectrum of knowledge learning goals. Furthermore, we systematically outline the processes of knowledge construction and optimization, analyze various architectural designs and learning strategies used to acquire representative and robust knowledge, and summarize recent applications in classification, recognition, and generation. Finally, we explore future research directions concerning architecture design, knowledge quality, and theoretical advancements in regression-based learning. By providing a thorough overview, this survey offers valuable insights and practical guidelines for both industry professionals and the academic community regarding Teacher-Student architectures in multi-objective knowledge learning. Furthermore, the insights gained from teacher-student frameworks can be applied to other multi-objective optimization problems. Finally, we provide a concise summary of the challenges and opportunities associated with teacher-student architectures for both knowledge learning and multi-task optimization. The source code for this survey can be accessed at: https://github.com/WSY2000/STS-Nets.
We introduce a new, compact representation for graphical models, a foundational framework for numerous reasoning tasks. These findings underscore the necessity of treating the loss function as a tunable hyperparameter rather than adopting it as a fixed default. To facilitate this, we have developed a versatile framework capable of testing any loss function across diverse datasets, which is available as an open-source Python library: https://github.com/significantfigures/ltf. Empirical Bayesian methods are another viable approach for hyperparameter tuning, particularly in scenarios with limited data where exhaustive grid searches are impractical. As demonstrated in this study, such methods effectively optimize discrete hyperparameters like categorical loss functions. We apply an empirical Bayesian strategy using a uniform prior over a discrete grid of candidates, resulting in a discrete posterior distribution that ranks the losses by their likelihood. This simple framework offers a rapid initial screening mechanism before conducting more granular searches on the most promising options. Although our evaluation focuses on supervised classification, this approach is easily adaptable to other domains. Furthermore, the methodology described here extends beyond loss functions to any discrete hyperparameter, and the associated source code is accessible via https://github.com/significantfigures/ltf.

From a practical perspective, this research has potential applications in network design and biological data analysis, such as constructing hierarchical clusterings from biological sequences. Regarding security, this line of inquiry could have implications for network security protocols and the encryption of biological information. In civil engineering, the findings might influence the design of networked infrastructure. Legally, a concept similar to resolvability was addressed in the US Cybersecurity Performance Standards. Ethically, research on metric dimension in graphs (including trees) has potential uses in locating missing individuals. Finally, regarding artificial intelligence and machine learning, this work relates to the metric embedding of graphs into other metric spaces.
Cardiac auscultation serves as a critical point-of-care technique for the early identification of heart conditions, yet the automatic analysis of heart sounds for detecting abnormalities is hindered by additive noise and sensor-specific degradation. This study proposes methods to tackle cardiac abnormality detection in the presence of both distortion types. Initially, we mathematically evaluate the impact of additive and convolutional noise on short-term filterbank features and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) layers. Guided by this analysis, we introduce a hybrid approach combining linear and logarithmic spectrogram-image features. These 2D representations are fed into a Residual CNN (ResNet) for detecting heart sound anomalies. Validation was conducted using an open-access dataset of noisy heart sounds recorded by various stethoscope sensors. The proposed method outperforms conventional techniques, achieving an AUC of 91.36%, an F-1 score of 84.09%, and a Macc of 85.08%. Furthermore, the approach demonstrates superior mean accuracy across diverse source domains, including variations in stethoscope types and noise levels, confirming its robustness under different recording conditions. By effectively mitigating the effects of background noise and sensor variability in phonocardiogram (PCG) classification, this combination of linear and logarithmic features with a ResNet classifier facilitates the development of computer-aided cardiac auscultation systems capable of operating in noisy environments using low-cost stethoscopes. This capability supports the early diagnosis of heart diseases through the automatic detection of abnormal heart sounds. Notably, during validation, the system was tested on a previously unseen dataset covering variations in noise types and stethoscope sources, underscoring its adaptability to different phonocardiogram sources. The source code and dataset for this method are accessible at: https://github.com/VivekKumar1999/Convo-Conv-ResNet. By enabling early detection of cardiovascular diseases via the automatic identification of pathological heart sounds, this research holds significant clinical value. Consequently, combining PCG-based classification with ECG analysis offers a comprehensive framework for classifying heart sounds and diagnosing cardiovascular conditions.
We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies with measured total luminosities for the two fine-structure transitions of neutral atomic carbon ($^{3}P_1 \rightarrow ^{3}P_{0}$ and $^{3}P_2 \rightarrow ^{3}P_{1}$), determining that their average excitation conditions are strongly subthermal. This conclusion was drawn from modeling the CI(2-1)/(1-0) ratios ($R^{(ci)}_{21/10}$) using exact solutions for a 3-level system, without relying on specific assumptions regarding the kinematic state of the associated $\rm H_2$ gas or the form of its cooling function. This modeling approach also enabled the estimation of $\rm T_{mk}$ (the maximum entropy temperature) for each galaxy. Consistent with prior findings, we observed a clear correlation between $R^{(ci)}_{21/10}$ and $\rm T_{mk}$, which allowed us to derive a mean relationship between these parameters for low-luminosity galaxies ($L'(\rm CO)(6/5) < 3 \times 10^{8}\,W_{\odot}$). For galaxies with higher $L'(\rm CO)(6/5)$, we identified a distinct bifurcation in the $T^{(ci)}_{mk}$ distributions for fixed $R^{(ci)}_{21/10}$ values, a phenomenon we attribute to variations in $\rm T_{mk}$ between the $\rm H_2$ gas responsible for the bright CO(6-5) emission and the interstellar medium probed by the CI fine structure lines. Extending the application of these empirical relations (derived here for the CI(2-1) line) to extragalactic volumes, we estimate that non-LTE excitation causes an underestimation of the total mass of both atomic ($M_{\rm CI}$) and molecular ($M_{\rm H_2}$) gas by a factor of three for typical star-forming dwarf galaxies and by an even larger margin for low-luminosity galaxies. Furthermore, the mean $T^{(ci)}_{mk}$ for our sample exhibits a strong correlation with $ \rm SFR / L'_ {CI}(1-0)$, supporting the hypothesis that $T^{(ci)}_{mk}$ serves as an effective tracer of the thermodynamic temperature of the cold interstellar medium in extragalactic environments.
We demonstrate that for ASEP with step initial conditions and a second-class particle originating at zero, the particle's velocity converges almost surely to a uniform distribution on $[-1,1]$ as time approaches infinity. This result affirmatively settles Conjectures 1.9 and 1.10 from [Amir, Angel and Valko, "The TASEP speed process", Annals of Probability 39, 1205--1242, 2011] and enables the construction of the ASEP speed process. Additionally, we establish that ASEP and its associated speed process satisfy a central limit theorem. Finally, utilizing the coupling of ASEP, its speed process, and TASEC, we show that a coalescence of second-class particles implies the convergence of both ASEP and its coupling to TASEP as $N$ tends to infinity. Notably, this convergence holds even if the TASEP particles start at positions $\nu_n(N)$, provided that $\nu_n(N)/N$ converges almost surely to a deterministic limit $v_n$ as $N \to \infty$ for each $n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$. As a consequence, we prove that a coalescence of second-class particles occurs with positive probability when $\nu_n(N) = \lfloor N v_n \rfloor$.
This study examines various mathematical models developed during the current pandemic to tackle key public health concerns regarding epidemic dynamics and their origins. We begin by outlining the fundamental characteristics of the classic Kermack-McKendrick models before exploring their generalizations and applications to contact networks, viral co-circulation, epidemic curve trajectories, probability distributions, and passage times required to define compartments in these models. Collectively, these examples underscore that a system of differential equations designed for a specific epidemiological challenge relies fundamentally on the epidemiological, medical, and biological context driving its formulation and analysis. Merely fitting differential models to data without considering biological feasibility may yield statistically significant results but will ultimately fail to offer actionable insights for managing, mitigating, or controlling the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. To conclude, we summarize several important considerations for constructing, constructing, and utilizing models in epidemiological research. By reviewing these fundamentals, we aim to encourage further development of models adapted to specific scenarios, such as veterinary, botanical, mycological, or other emerging infectious diseases like Ebola, Zika, Dengue, Lassa fever, Lyme disease, influenza, and HIV/AIDS. Additionally, this overview provides necessary background for integrating stochastic processes, examining threshold behaviors, investigating stable limit cycles, conducting bifurcation analyses, optimizing resource allocation, performing cost-benefit evaluations, carrying out risk assessments through decision theory, and utilizing game theory approaches. Ultimately, this survey serves as an introduction to a forthcoming comprehensive handbook on infectious disease modeling. In the face of an ongoing global crisis, there is an urgent need to prioritize basic research, ensure adequate supply chains for medical resources, and invest in the development of vaccines and therapeutic medications.
It remains uncertain if bulge expansion causes the flattening of the star-forming main sequence (MS) at high masses. To examine how bulges influence the MS, we analyzed the NUV$-r$ color—a reliable tracer of specific star formation rate—in the central ($r<R_{50}$) versus outer regions of 6,401 local star-forming galaxies. Our results show that for galaxies with $M_{\ast}<10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ is only about 0.25 magnitudes redder than the outer regions. However, above $M_{\ast}=10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ becomes significantly redder than the outer regions, indicating that bulges in massive galaxies are more evolved. When sorting galaxies by S\'ersic index $n$, those with $n$>2.0 exhibit redder central NUV$-r$ colors than those with $n$<2.0, even when controlling for B/T ratio and $M_{\ast}$. This implies that bulge star formation depends more strongly on $n$ (or central mass density) than on the B/T ratio. Furthermore, the fraction of galaxies with $n$>2.0 rises sharply with mass for $M_{\ast}>10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, aligning with the turnover in the MS at this transition mass. We conclude that the growing proportion of low specific star formation rate, dense bulges in galaxies with $M_{\ast}>10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, rather than an increase in B/T, drives the flattening of the $M_{\ast}$$-$SFR relation at high masses. This supports the hypothesis that the $n$>2.0 bulge population defines the upper mass limit for giant elliptical galaxies. To further isolate the impact of $n$ from B/T, we will soon present the results from a simulation using a novel "swapping" technique.
This research conducts a cross-lingual sentiment analysis of news articles by applying zero-shot and few-shot learning techniques. The objective is to categorize Croatian news into positive, negative, and neutral sentiments using a Slovene dataset. The proposed system utilizes a trilingual BERT-based model trained on English, Slovene, and Croatian. The study evaluates various configurations using two-language datasets and introduces a straightforward multi-task model for sentiment classification. Assessments are carried out across single-task and multi-task experiments within both few-shot and zero-shot scenarios for Croatian and Slovene. Findings indicate that the trilingual BERT model outperforms traditional CNN and RNN models. Furthermore, the data results demonstrate that single-task performance in few-shot learning is surpassed by the multi-task model. Notably, the single-stream T-BERT model achieved the highest performance in both few-shot and zero-shot learning for Croatian and Slovene. Overall, this research highlights the effectiveness of transformer-based models, specifically BERT, in sentiment classification for low-resource languages. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/evamarijarus/ZRSNA.
This study reports the potential detection of a nonmonotonic radial rotation profile in a low-mass, low-luminosity giant star. While low- and intermediate-mass stars typically exhibit rigid rotation on the main sequence, stellar evolution into the giant phase—characterized by core contraction and envelope expansion—generally predicts a profile with a rapidly rotating core and a slower envelope and surface. KIC 9267654, however, displays a surface rotation rate exceeding that of its bulk envelope, contradicting standard angular momentum conservation expectations. We enhance the spectroscopic constraints on the surface rotation, confirm that pulsation frequencies align with previously determined core and envelope rotation rates, and establish that the star lacks significant chemical peculiarities. Furthermore, we evaluate evidence against the presence of a tidally interacting companion. Finally, we explore possible origins for this anomalous rotation profile, such as the accretion of a giant planet or anomalous angular momentum transport via tidal inertial waves driven by a close substellar companion, and advocate for additional observational and theoretical investigations.
Fake news spreads rapidly across social media, reaching global audiences and endangering communities. While deep learning models perform well on labeled data for specific events, their efficacy often drops when encountering new events due to domain shifts. This creates a significant hurdle for existing detection systems when dealing with emergent events where large, labeled datasets are scarce. Furthermore, adapting to new events typically requires training a model from scratch or extensive fine-tuning, which is often costly, impractical, and difficult to sustain in real-world scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we introduce MetaFEND, an end-to-end framework designed to rapidly learn fake news detection for emerging events using only a small number of verified posts. By combining meta-learning with neural process methods, our approach leverages the strengths of both techniques. Specifically, we incorporate a label embedding module and a hard attention mechanism to better manage categorical data and filter out irrelevant content. Extensive experiments on multimedia datasets from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate that MetaFEND effectively detects fake news in previously unseen events, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. The source code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/ckck1998/MetaFEND.
Golay complementary matrices (GCM) have recently attracted significant attention due to their potential applications in omnidirectional precoding. In this paper, we extend GCMs to multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays (GCA) and introduce new construction methods for GCA pairs and quads. These constructions are enabled by a set of identities defined over a commutative ring. We demonstrate that a quaternary quads construction is feasible when the product of the array sizes equals a quaternary quads number, removing any other constraints on the dimensions. Furthermore, we propose a ternary construction that is valid for any quaternary quads number. Leveraging a recent random construction, we establish quaternary quads numbers up to $17\times10^6$ and propose potential constructions for quads over $10^8$. Finally, to validate the utility of quaternary quads in omnidirectional precoding, we design quaternary quads matrix quads for the specific size combination $2\times1$, $2\times3$, $2\times5$, and $2\times7$.
Laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) represents a new minimally invasive approach for ablating intracranial structures to manage mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE). Automating lesion quantification through pre- and post-treatment region of interest (ROI) segmentation offers an objective means to evaluate therapeutic efficacy. While deep learning methods, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), represent the current standard for ROI segmentation, they depend heavily on extensive annotated datasets, which are difficult to gather for emerging procedures like LITT. To address this limitation, we introduce a Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis Framework (PAVAE) designed to increase both the volume and variety of training data. This framework comprises two sequential networks: a mask synthesis network and a mask-guided lesion synthesis network. To leverage extrinsic information for enhanced supervision, we developed a condition embedding block (CEB) and a mask embedding block (MEB) that encode intrinsic mask characteristics into the feature space. Ultimately, a segmentation network was trained on a combination of raw and synthetic lesion images to assess the framework's efficacy. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach generates realistic synthetic images and significantly improves the performance of downstream segmentation tasks compared to conventional data augmentation methods. Furthermore, the framework proves particularly beneficial when the initial dataset size is limited. The source code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/taoli1997/PAVAE.
Feature extraction serves as an effective strategy for mitigating dimensionality challenges inherent in high-dimensional datasets. Given the recent surge in interest toward contrastive learning as a prominent self-supervised technique, this study introduces a unified framework grounded in a novel perspective of contrastive learning (CL), applicable to both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework initially establishes two distinct CL graphs to precisely define positive and negative pairs, followed by the determination of a projection matrix through the minimization of a contrastive loss function. Furthermore, the approach integrates both similar and dissimilar samples to harmonize unsupervised and supervised extraction processes. Specifically, the study proposes three methodologies: an unsupervised contrastive learning approach, along with two distinct supervised contrastive learning methods. Extensive numerical experiments conducted across five real-world datasets confirm that the proposed framework outperforms existing methods. These results demonstrate that minimizing contrastive loss is a potent technique that can be optimized via various mechanisms to enhance feature extraction quality. Additionally, the findings indicate that utilizing similar and dissimilar samples for supervised contrastive learning does not necessarily yield superior outcomes. The approach detailed in this work emphasizes the minimization of contrastive loss coupled with an additional optimization technique, rather than the incorporation of similar and dissimilar samples. Specifically, the methodology combines either centralization or random projection with the minimization of contrastive loss for its two proposed methods. To access the author versions of this work and associated supplementary materials, visit the following link: https://doi.org/10.4209/lee.19072. The repository address is http://dx.doi.org/10.4209/lee.19072.
Although large language models (LLMs) achieve human-level performance across many natural language tasks, it remains unclear whether they absorb knowledge more effectively from structured sources like knowledge graphs (KGs) or from unstructured text. This study introduces a technique to embed structured knowledge into LLMs by directly training T5 models on factual triples extracted from knowledge graphs. Our results demonstrate that T5 models pre-trained on Wikidata using this approach surpass standard baselines on FreebaseQA, WikiHop, and specific subsets of TriviaQA and NaturalQuestions. Furthermore, models trained on factual triples perform comparably to those trained on natural language sentences containing identical information. When applied to the smaller WikiMovies dataset, our method achieved a threefold increase in exact match scores on the MetaQA task relative to the T5 baseline. A key benefit of this approach is that it eliminates the need for aligning knowledge graphs with text corpora during data preparation, rendering it especially advantageous for industry-scale knowledge graphs. Additionally, because the method relies solely on factual triples, it is agnostic to the specific domain or schema of the underlying knowledge graph. Ultimately, our findings suggest that large scale alone is insufficient for LLMs to internalize external knowledge effectively; rather, a combination of large scale and targeted training data yields superior outcomes. This work underscores the potential of leveraging knowledge graphs to enhance large language models.
Non-linear interactions between electromagnetic fields (EMF) arise due to vacuum polarization within quantum electrodynamics (QED). Such interactions suggest that non-linear electrodynamics could significantly impact black hole physics. This study examines the connection between the observable shadow radius and the first-order phase transition of non-linear charged AdS black holes within the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. The analysis reveals that, under specific conditions, the shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature (or pressure) exhibit non-monotonic behaviors. Furthermore, from the perspective of the shadow radius, the phase transition temperature is higher than that derived from the horizon radius under identical conditions. These findings suggest that the shadow radius serves as an effective probe for uncovering thermodynamic phase transition details in black holes. Additionally, thermal profiles illustrating the coexistence of big and small black hole phases during phase transitions are presented for both the shadow radius and temperature. Finally, the influence of the non-linearity parameter on the shadow radius, specific heat, and thermal phase transition is explored. Finally, a phase diagram derived from the specific heat is constructed to summarize the study's key conclusions. The research is available on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00645.

While numerous reconstruction methods exist—from conventional protocols to machine learning approaches—no single universal technique currently allows for extracting the Wigner function from the optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that nonclassical phenomena, including entanglement variations during dynamical evolution and the emergence of quantum synchronization, manifest as qualitative shifts within the optical tomograms themselves. Consequently, explicit state reconstruction is unnecessary to detect these effects. We highlight this principle and provide direct evidence within the optical tomograms for three specific scenarios: (i) the EPR state, (ii) a dynamical entanglement transition occurring in an optical Bose-Hubbard model, and (iii) the development of quantum synchronization within a system of interacting lasers coupled through a common bus waveguide. Generally, constructing the submodule lattice $L(M)$ for a specific module $M$ poses significant challenges. While R. P. Stanley proposed in \cite{St} a technique to build a distributive lattice from its join irreducibles, determining all such irreducible submodules remains a difficult undertaking. For multiplicity-free modules $M$, we introduce an adaptation of Stanley's approach grounded in the composition factors of $M$. This method requires a collection of submodules $A_1,\ldots , A_n$ with known lattice structures that encompass all of $M$'s composition factors, enabling the reconstruction of $L(M)$. We demonstrate this procedure for a series of Verma modules $M(\gl_n)$, where $n$ is a positive integer, associated with the Lie superalgebra $\osp(3,2)$. Our results indicate that for $n\ge 2$, the lattice $L(M(\gl_n))$ is isomorphic to the (extended) free distributive lattice of rank 3. Consequently, these findings imply that multiplicity-free modules do not always possess relatively simple submodule lattices. Additionally, we examine whether the inclusion of the highest composable triple formsets on an set of size $n$ into the definition of Verma modules for $\osp(q,p)$ alters their submodule lattices. Finally, we consider whether replacing simple modules in the "basis" of the basis-formset with verifiable lattices of multiplicity-free modules induces an isomorphic extended basis-formset. We provide examples illustrating both affirmative and negative outcomes for this last inquiry. Verma modules and their submodule lattices for the Lie superalgebra $\osp(q,p)$ are investigated in \cite{CL}, \cite{Ch}, \cite{Ch2}, and the current work. Furthermore, the study of submodule lattices for various other modules can be found in \cite{CKLR}, \cite{D}, \cite{H}, \cite{MS}, and \cite{SW}.
This study demonstrates that certain well-established recurrent operators—specifically the recurrent curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators—play a crucial role in determining whether biharmonic hypersurfaces are minimal. The findings indicate that under specific conditions, if a hypersurface exhibits any of these recurrent operators, it must be a circular tube embedded within a minimal Lagrangian hypersurface within a light-like Kundt spacane. Additionally, the paper examines biharmonic minimal ruled surfaces defined in a Sasakian space form. Ultimately, the conclusion highlights that for a recurrent curvature operator on an extrinsic symmetric hypersurface in a light-like Kundt spacane, the hypersurface constitutes a circular tube within an affine light-like ruled surface found in a Sasakian space form. Furthermore, an open problem concerning extrinsic symmetric hypersurfaces in light-like Kundt spacanes is discussed and addressed. Ultimately, if a hypersurface in such a spacane possesses an invariant almost light-like plane field and its extrinsic symmetry operator aligns with the recurrence of the curvature operator, it forms a circular tube within a minimal Lagrangian hypersurface in that same spacane.

The image of this function is denoted by $N_{p/q}$. While $N_{p/q}$ encompasses all nonnegative integers, existing literature typically concentrates on the subset of words evaluating to these integers; this set forms a chaotic, non-context-free language. In contrast, this work examines subsets of $(N_{p/q})^d$ that are $p/q$-recognisable, meaning they can be recognized by finite automata operating over $(A_p)^d$. First, we provide a characterization of these sets as those definable within a specific first-order logic, drawing a parallel to the B\"uchi-Bruy\`ere Theorem for integer-based numeration systems. Second, we demonstrate that neither the natural ordering relation nor the modulo-$q$ operator are $p/q$-recognisable. Finally, we establish that a direct product of two finite automata over $A_p$ is not necessarily $p/q$-recognisable. These findings highlight significant distinctions between integer and rational base numeration systems. Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data with an integrated luminosity of 1.7 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb detector, the differential decay rate for the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ process is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This decay is identified via the subsequent decays $D_s^{*-}\rightarrow D_s^{-}\gamma$ and $D_s^{-}\rightarrow K^-K^+\pi^-$. The extracted differential decay rate is analyzed using the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert (CLN) and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed (BGL) parametrisations to determine the corresponding form factor quantities. At the average hadron recoil, the CLN and BGL results yield $|h_d(\rho_{had})^{1/2}\xi(q^2_{dec})|=0.47\pm0.14(\text{exp})\pm0.06(\text{sys})\pm0.09(\text{theor})$ and $0.47\pm0.14(\text{exp})\pm0.09(\text{sys})\pm0.08(\text{theor})$, respectively. These findings align with prior LHCb measurements of this and related decay processes.
This study tackles the persistent challenge of extracting dynamical information from noisy acoustic emission signals generated by an adhesive tape being peeled under a constant traction velocity. By applying a phase space reconstruction method, we confirm deterministic chaotic dynamics through the identification of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent within a specific range of traction speeds. These findings are interpreted using a model that underscores the deterministic nature of acoustic emissions by linking them to stick-slip dynamics. Notably, the correlation dimension and Lyapunov exponent vanish outside the chaotic regime, indicating that these metrics serve as effective indicators for detecting chaotic dynamics and transitioning between different dynamical states. To achieve phase space reconstruction and derive the correlation dimension and Lyapunov exponent, the signal is filtered to isolate acoustic emissions and is subsequently scaled to enhance the clarity of attractor visualization in phase space; however, these same processing steps introduce artifacts that conceal the underlying causes of the acoustic emissions themselves.
In the early 1930s, K. Menger explored the concept of an abstract angle function, defining it broadly for metric and semi-metric spaces. He also formulated two challenges regarding the conformal embeddability of spaces equipped with an angle function into Euclidean spaces. Although these problems garnered attention later, solutions were limited to specific instances of metric spaces. This article updates the definition of the angle function to accommodate a broader class of spaces characterized by a betweenness relation, which we consider a more natural framework. Within this generalized setting, we resolve both problems originally posed by Menger. Furthermore, we establish that embeddability into Euclidean spaces implies embeddability into Hilbert spaces, detailing the conditions required for such an embedding. Finally, we define a betweenness function for spaces with a betweenness relation and analyze its properties, concluding with an exploration of the unique existence of the betweenness function in spaces that are embeddable into Euclidean spaces. Our findings indicate that a betweenness function exists for such spaces if and only if they satisfy the quadrangle inequality. Additionally, we highlight the utility of the betweenness function in addressing the positive curvature problem for metric spaces.
Neural network-based point cloud models have achieved significant success and are extensively utilized in safety-critical domains, including Lidar recognition systems for autonomous vehicles. Nevertheless, these models remain susceptible to adversarial attacks designed to deceive predictions through stealthy semantic transformations like rotation and tapering. This paper introduces TPC, a transformation-specific smoothing framework that delivers tight and scalable robustness guarantees for point cloud models against such attacks. We begin by classifying common 3D transformations into three groups: additive (e.g., shearing), composable (e.g., rotation), and indirectly composable (e.g., tapering), offering generic robustness certification strategies for each category. Subsequently, we define specialized certification protocols for various specific semantic transformations and their combinations. Extensive experiments on multiple common 3D transformations demonstrate that TPC significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods; for instance, our framework increases certified accuracy against twisting transformations along the z-axis (within 20°) from 20.3% to 83.8%. The source code and models are accessible at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.
The verification techniques of formal methods are now being applied to program testing, with the goal of enhancing the reliability of software development, testing, and evolution. Our geometric theory of testing serves as the specification for a testing environment, which functions as the final stage of a toolchain designed to assist professional developers, hobbyists, and computer science students. This environment features an automated algorithm that identifies errors within executed tests and guides their correction by displaying a stick diagram of causal execution chains on a screen. Users can navigate this diagram backward, similar to using a satnav to follow roads on a map, which highlights the specific locations in the code that require modification to eliminate the error. In this presentation, I will describe the theory, demonstrate how a text-based execution chain functions as a type check, and show an example of a stik diagram for a complex execution chain. Additionally, I will outline a proof theory and present a theorem that defines the properties of a testable system.
This paper presents an explicit formulation of the weight component of Serre's conjecture for GL_2, grounded in Kummer theory and deliberately avoiding p-adic Hodge theory. The approach relies on characterizing the reduction modulo p of crystalline extensions via specific "G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles" and applying Abrashkin's result, which relates these cocycles to Kummer theory. While Dembele-Diamond-Roberts previously offered an explicit formulation using local class field theory (for the unramified case) and the second author did so in the general case, we demonstrate that their description can be derived directly from ours through the explicit reciprocity laws established by Brueckner, Shafarevich, and Vostokov. These computations highlight how our reliance on Kummer theory sidesteps specific combinatorial complexities found in those earlier works. Furthermore, we illustrate how the proposed formulation can be implemented computationally using PARI/GP. Finally, we sketch potential extensions of this method to higher-dimensional units and Galois representations. The appendix collaborates with J. S. Guerin to review fundamental concepts regarding Hodge-Tate weights and crystalline representations. His research specifically explores the Serre conjecture and Kummer theory concerning L-adic representations of the absolute Galois group. Advancements in technology have enabled big data processing, yet this has created substantial computational challenges when solving large-scale linear systems or performing matrix inversions. This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm derived from the NS, termed "Nested Neumann" (NN). This approach generalizes higher-order iterations of NI and CI by leveraging a computationally efficient iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, dependent on a specified "inception depth." Mathematical analysis confirms that the NN method: (i) converges provided the preconditioning matrix satisfies the spectral norm condition required for NS, (ii) achieves a convergence rate equivalent to an order of (inception depth plus one), and (iii) performs optimally with an inception depth of one or two, contingent upon available RAM. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for NN suitable for massive sparse matrices, accounting for increased computational costs. Crucially, we establish an analytical equivalence between NS and NN (including NI, CI, and higher orders), a finding particularly relevant for mMIMO systems. Finally, the NN method is applicable to positive semi-definite matrices for inversion and can be utilized for any linear system, whether sparse, non-sparse, or complex. Extensive numerical experiments using non-sparse matrices up to 20,000 by 20,000 and real-world scenarios, including sound source localization and massive MIMO wireless systems, demonstrate that NN significantly outperforms conventional approximate iterative methods, approaching the speed of direct inversion methods. The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism dependent on rapid gas cooling, potentially active in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. This study employs linear analysis to quantify how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. We developed a cooling timescale model incorporating dust growth beyond micron scales and size-dependent settling. By integrating this model with linear stability analysis, we identified the "VSI zone" and calculated the maximum growth rate at various radial distances. Our results indicate that both dust growth and settling restrict the VSI zone to the immediate vicinity of the midplane. Consequently, the instability's growth rate diminishes because the vertical shear of rotational velocity—the instability's driving force—is weaker at lower altitudes. In our default model of a 0.01 solar mass disk, dust growth from 10 microns to 1 mm reduces the growth rate by a factor exceeding 10. Ultimately, the suppression of VSI-driven turbulence by dust evolution could accelerate further dust processing in outer disk regions and account for the significant dust settling observed in the HL Tau system. To explore the interplay between dust evolution and other hydrodynamical instabilities, as well as dust growth and fragmentation, we introduce a standardized numerical framework for disk models accessible at https://github.com/outerdiskmodels/odm.

This work addresses the challenge of a Parameter Server (PS) learning a model from data distributed across graph nodes, with Federated Learning (FL) serving as the primary application. A significant hurdle in FL is the communication bottleneck between nodes and the PS. Although performing multiple local updates per iteration before syncing with the PS is a common strategy to alleviate this bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of node-specific data often results in biased models and delayed convergence. To overcome both communication and data heterogeneity issues, we investigate Random Walk (RW) learning algorithms. These algorithms utilize direct connections between nodes, which are typically more efficient than communicating with the PS. In this framework, the model acts as a "baton" passed iteratively to a neighboring node after each update. Designing effective RW algorithms is complicated by data heterogeneity and uncertainty regarding data distributions; ideally, nodes with more informative data should be visited more frequently. We formulate this as a sleeping multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem to develop a near-optimal node sampling strategy that minimizes gradient estimate variance and asymptotically approaches optimal sampling. Building on this, we propose an adaptive random walk learning algorithm and provide theoretical convergence guarantees. Our numerical experiments confirm these theoretical results and demonstrate that our algorithm surpasses existing random walk methods. Furthermore, we conduct a meta-analysis of various random walk learning algorithms to highlight their strengths and limitations. The code for our methods can be accessed at https://github.com/nrsharma/Federated-Random-Walk-Learning.
